passage: The word improvisation tends to conjure an image of pure spontaneity: a musician who sits down with nothing prepared and lets whatever arrives come out. Listeners who admire improvisers often praise them in exactly these terms, as if the value of the performance lay in its having come from nowhere. Yet the image badly misdescribes what improvising musicians actually do. In the classical traditions of the Indian subcontinent, a performer exploring a raga is bound by an intricate set of expectations: which notes may be used, how the scale is approached in ascent and in descent, which phrases characterise the raga and which would make it sound like a neighbouring one. A jazz soloist working through a familiar tune is likewise held by the sequence of chords beneath the melody, by the length of each chorus and by a large shared stock of phrases that players absorb over years of listening.

What these traditions share is not an absence of rules but a particular relation to them. The improviser has internalised the constraints so thoroughly that they no longer need to be consulted; they shape choices in the way grammar shapes the sentences of a fluent speaker, who does not pause to recall the rules before talking. The comparison with language is useful because it removes an apparent paradox. Nobody thinks that a conversation is unoriginal because it obeys grammar, and nobody thinks that grammar prevents people from saying things that have never been said before. On the contrary, it is the shared structure that makes a new sentence intelligible as new.

This has a practical consequence for how improvisation is learned. A student who is told simply to be free usually produces something shapeless, or falls back on a handful of habits picked up by accident. Teachers in both traditions instead begin with imitation: the student copies phrases, sometimes for years, until the vocabulary becomes second nature. To an outsider this can look like the opposite of creativity. But imitation here is the means by which the constraints are absorbed, and only once they have been absorbed can the student vary them with confidence.

None of this is to say that improvisation is merely the recombination of stored parts, or that the best improvisers are simply those with the largest memories. What listeners value in a great performance is often a moment at which a convention is stretched or bent in a way that still makes sense within the tradition, so that the surprise is felt as a surprise. Such moments are possible only for someone who knows exactly where the boundaries lie. Freedom in improvisation, in other words, is not freedom from form but a fluency so complete that form can be played with.

passage: Public debate about bureaucracy tends to oscillate between two complaints. One is that officials are rigid, applying rules mechanically to people whose circumstances the rules never anticipated. The other is that officials are arbitrary, treating similar applicants differently according to mood, prejudice or the length of the queue. The usual remedy for the second complaint is more rules: tighter eligibility criteria, standard forms, checklists that leave nothing to judgement. Each new scandal of favouritism produces another layer of instructions, and the layers accumulate. The remedy is seldom questioned, because it seems obvious that a rule applied uniformly is fairer than a person deciding as he pleases.

What this remedy overlooks is that the officials who deal directly with the public, the benefits clerk, the housing inspector, the teacher deciding which pupil needs extra help, cannot stop exercising judgement however detailed their instructions become. A rule says that an applicant must provide proof of address; it does not say how hard the clerk should look for an acceptable document when the applicant has been living with relatives. Moreover, such officials almost always have more cases than time. They must decide whose file to open first, whose story to probe and whose to accept, and these decisions shape outcomes as surely as any formal ruling. When rules are tightened, judgement does not disappear. It retreats into these less visible choices, where it is harder to observe and correct.

This is not to romanticise frontline discretion. The same latitude that allows a sympathetic clerk to find a way through for a desperate family allows an unsympathetic one to find reasons for delay, and there is ample reason to think that such latitude is not exercised evenly across applicants of different backgrounds. The case for discretion is not that officials can be trusted. It is that the choice is not between discretion and its absence, but between discretion that is acknowledged and discretion that is driven underground. Discretion of the first kind can be examined and improved; discretion of the second kind can only be suspected.

Seen this way, the task of administrative reform changes. Instead of writing rules ever more finely in the hope of closing every gap, an agency might record the informal decisions its staff actually make, review samples of cases to see how similar applicants fare, and give officials explicit guidance on the purposes their judgement should serve. None of these steps would remove judgement from the counter; they would make it something an agency can see, discuss and, where necessary, correct. Such measures concede what the rule-writer prefers to deny: that every system of rules ends, at its edges, in someone deciding.

passage: When a welfare benefit goes unclaimed by many of the people entitled to it, the usual explanation is that they did not know about it, did not need it badly enough or could not be bothered. The explanation locates the problem in the claimant. It rarely asks what claiming actually involves: discovering that the benefit exists, working out whether one qualifies, gathering documents that may be held by three different offices, completing a form whose questions assume a settled address and a regular income, and then, often, doing it all again a few months later to prove that nothing has changed.

These demands are usually described as administrative friction, an unfortunate but neutral by-product of running any large programme. They are not neutral. Every hour required to claim is an hour that some people can spare more easily than others, and the people least able to spare it are frequently those the programme was meant to help: the seriously ill, those working irregular shifts, those for whom scarcity has already consumed much of the attention that form-filling demands. A requirement that costs a comfortable applicant an afternoon may cost a struggling one the benefit itself.

There is a further reason to look closely at such burdens. Because they are set through forms, procedures and office hours rather than through legislation, they can change who receives a benefit without any public decision that it should. A government that wished to spend less on a programme but did not wish to say so could add a document to the list or shorten the period for renewal, and the number of recipients would fall while the rules of entitlement stayed exactly as they were. Whether or not anyone intends this, the effect is a form of policy made out of sight, insulated from the debate that a change in the law would provoke.

This is not to say that verification is illegitimate. Public programmes depend on the belief that money goes to those entitled to it, and some checking sustains that belief among the taxpayers who fund them. But the costs of checking are borne in two places, in the office and in the lives of applicants, and only the first tends to be counted. A sound design would weigh the time and strain imposed on claimants as seriously as the cost of the errors it prevents, and would treat a large gap between entitlement and receipt as evidence about the system rather than about the people outside it.

passage: Thought experiments occupy an awkward place in the theory of knowledge. Scientists and philosophers have long used them to settle questions, and some of the most admired episodes in the history of physics turn on an imagined scenario rather than an actual measurement. Yet a thought experiment, by definition, collects no new data. The experimenter sits still and imagines. If we learn something about the world this way, it is not obvious where the information comes from, and two answers have dominated discussion.

According to the first, a thought experiment is an argument in disguise. Its vivid scenario can always be rewritten as a set of premises and a conclusion, and whatever it teaches, it teaches because the premises were already believed and the conclusion follows from them. The imagery is persuasive packaging, useful perhaps for teaching, but adding nothing to the logical content. According to the second, the best thought experiments give us something no argument could: a kind of direct intellectual insight into the necessary structure of nature, as if the mind could see a law of physics in the way the eye sees a colour.

Neither answer fits the most celebrated example well. Galileo asked his readers to imagine a heavy body and a light one tied together and dropped. If heavier bodies fall faster, as the received physics of his day held, the light body should hold back the heavy one, so that the pair falls more slowly than the heavy body alone; but the pair is heavier than the heavy body, so it should fall faster. The supposition contradicts itself, and the natural way out is that all bodies fall at the same rate, at least in the absence of a resisting medium. The argument reading can reconstruct this, but only by writing in premises that no one had formulated before the scenario was imagined: for instance, that the speed of a composite body must lie somewhere between the speeds of its parts. The insight reading, for its part, makes the result mysterious, as though Galileo had glimpsed a law rather than noticed a contradiction in what he and his readers already believed.

A better account is that thought experiments work by drawing on knowledge we have but have never made explicit. Everyone who has carried a load or watched things fall has a large stock of tacit expectations about how bodies behave. A well-constructed scenario brings these expectations to bear on a case where they collide with an explicit theory, and so exposes a tension that was there all along. What is new is not the information but its arrangement. This explains why thought experiments can be genuinely informative without new data, and also why they cannot be reduced to an argument that someone might have written down beforehand: the premises are found by running the scenario, not before it.

It also explains when they should not be trusted. Our tacit expectations were formed in a narrow band of experience, among objects of moderate size moving at moderate speeds. A thought experiment that asks us to imagine the very small, the very fast or the very distant invites us to apply those expectations where they were never tested, and the resulting conviction, however vivid, carries only the authority of the experience behind it. The method is neither a trick of rhetoric nor a window onto necessity. It is a way of interrogating what we already know, and it is exactly as reliable as that knowledge.

passage: The maxim that there is no disputing about taste is usually offered as a courtesy. When two people disagree about a film or a piece of music, one of them, sensing that the conversation is about to turn sour, observes that it is all a matter of taste, and the other, relieved, agrees. The maxim seems to express a modern and admirable humility, for who is anyone to tell another person what to enjoy? But the courtesy rests on a confusion, and the confusion has consequences for the way we talk about art and, in the end, for the way we treat one another.

The confusion is between preference and judgement. If you dislike the taste of coriander and I like it, there is nothing for us to argue about. Neither of us thinks the other has missed something; we simply report different reactions, and the reports do not compete, any more than your being cold and my being warm in the same room amounts to a disagreement about the room. Disagreements about novels or buildings are rarely like this. When I say that a novel is sentimental and you say that it is moving, each of us means to be saying something about the book, and each of us expects the other to be able, at least in principle, to recognise it. We point to passages, compare the novel with others, and draw attention to what the other may have overlooked. These are the moves of people who believe there is something to be right about, even if neither of them can prove it.

The relativist replies that this behaviour, however common, rests on an illusion. There is no fact about the book's sentimentality independent of readers' reactions, the argument runs, and so our disputes, unlike disputes about the boiling point of water, can never be settled; at most one party tires and gives up. This reply assumes that a dispute is worth having only if it can end in proof. Aesthetic argument, however, does not aim at proof. It aims at a change in perception, and its success is the moment when you look again at the passage I have pointed to and hear the false note I heard, or when I, rereading it at your insistence, find that what I took for manipulation is in fact restraint. Such moments are not rare. Most people can remember a friend, a teacher or a critic who showed them something they had not been able to see, and they do not remember the experience as having been talked into a preference; they remember it as having learned something.

It must be granted that some disagreements reach a floor. Two careful readers may agree about every feature of a poem, its rhythm, its imagery, its debts and its departures, and still differ about whether it is good, because one prizes austerity and the other abundance. At this point argument may genuinely run out, and it is sensible to say so. But the floor lies far lower than the maxim implies. Most disputes about taste break off long before they reach it, not because the parties have exhausted their reasons, but because one of them has invoked the maxim in order to end the conversation.

There is, finally, something less humble in the maxim than it appears. To tell someone that their view of a novel is merely a matter of taste is to decline to treat it as a view at all, that is, as a claim that might be true and from which one might learn. The maxim protects both parties from the risk of being wrong, but it does so at the price of the possibility of being changed. Real respect for another person's judgement would consist in disputing it.

passage: Debt is described, almost everywhere, in moral vocabulary. We speak of honouring our debts and of meeting our obligations, while default is treated as a failure of character and the borrower who cannot pay is presumed to have been improvident. These words are old, and they carry the experience of every society that has had to persuade strangers to trust one another across time. The language is not wholly misplaced, since a promise to repay is a promise, and a society in which such promises were lightly broken would soon find that no one would lend at all.

The moral framing, however, assigns the whole of the responsibility to one side of what is a two-sided contract. A loan is made by a lender who chose to lend, who estimated the chance of not being repaid and built that chance into the rate of interest, and who has been paid, in that higher rate, for bearing exactly the risk that sometimes comes to pass. When a borrower defaults, the risk for which the lender was compensated has simply materialised. To treat default as a sin rather than as an outcome the contract foresaw is to let lenders collect the premium for risk while disowning the risk itself.

This asymmetry has practical consequences. Where the moral framing is strong, lenders come under less pressure to judge carefully whether a borrower can repay, since any failure will be laid at the borrower's door, and borrowers in difficulty may conceal their distress out of shame instead of seeking to renegotiate early, when a settlement would cost both parties least. A lender that knows blame will travel in only one direction has in effect been relieved of part of the cost of its own mistakes, and an institution relieved of that cost can be expected to make more of them. The bankruptcy law of many countries embodies a different view: it treats a fresh start for an honest debtor as a social good, partly on the practical ground that a person crushed by debts that can never be paid produces little for anyone, creditors included.

None of this licenses casual default, and a borrower who spends money he never meant to return has done wrong in the plainest sense. The point is that obligation runs in both directions: the borrower owes repayment, and the lender owes care in deciding to lend. A moral language that recognised both duties would not be softer than the one we have; it would simply be more accurate about where responsibility lies when a loan goes bad.

passage: The line between literary and genre fiction is usually drawn in terms of freedom. The literary novel, it is said, invents its own shape, while the crime novel, the romance and the tale of space travel arrive with their shapes already supplied: a body in the first chapter, an obstacle between the lovers, a voyage, a crisis and a return. To write in a genre is, on this account, to fill in a form someone else designed, and the best a genre writer can hope for is to fill it in with unusual skill. Critics who accept this account tend to praise a crime novel by saying that it rises above its genre, as though the genre were something to be escaped.

The account has the logic of constraint backwards. Nobody thinks a sonnet a lesser poem because its length and rhyme scheme were fixed before the poet began. We understand that the fixed form is what makes certain effects possible: a turn in the ninth line registers as a turn only because the reader knows where turns are expected. Genre conventions work in much the same way. A reader of detective stories knows that the culprit must be among the people introduced, that the clues must be fair, that a solution will come. These expectations are not a cage around the writer but an instrument she can play, and the slightest departure from them, a detective who is wrong, a solution that satisfies the law but not the reader, is felt with a precision no unconventional novel can command, because the unconventional novel has no settled expectation to depart from.

This is also why devoted readers of a genre are often its most exacting critics. Having read a hundred novels built on the same frame, they are alert to the smallest variation in it, much as a chess player who knows an opening thoroughly notices a single unusual move that a novice would pass over. Such readers can tell at once whether a twist is earned or merely borrowed, and they are rarely generous to a writer who mistakes one for the other. Their pleasure is not the passive pleasure of repetition but the active one of comparison.

None of this rescues every genre book. Conventions harden into formula when a writer treats them as a checklist to be completed rather than an expectation to be worked against, and a great deal of genre fiction is written in exactly this way. But the same is true of literary fiction, which has its own conventions, the quiet revelation in the final paragraph, the fractured chronology, the unnamed narrator, and its own writers who complete them dutifully. The useful distinction is not between books that have conventions and books that lack them, since none lack them, but between books that do something with their conventions and books that merely obey them.

passage: A common modern objection to traditional mourning customs is that they put grief on a timetable. Many traditions mark fixed days after a death, often a gathering within the first two weeks, another around the fortieth day and a final observance at the first anniversary, and for centuries some communities prescribed the clothes a widow might wear and the months during which she should not appear at celebrations. To a sensibility that prizes authentic feeling, this looks like an intrusion: grief, it is said, is personal, it follows no calendar, and nobody has the right to tell a bereaved person when to stop.

The objection contains a truth, but it misreads what the calendar was for. The fixed days rarely claimed to measure how long sorrow lasts. What they did was settle a set of practical questions that otherwise fall, at the worst possible moment, on the people least able to answer them. When should relatives visit, and when should they leave? What is it acceptable to say? When may the household resume ordinary work without seeming callous? A prescribed sequence answers all of these in advance, so that the bereaved are spared the labour of inventing their own conduct while they are exhausted, and so that neighbours know when their presence is expected.

In this sense the timetable was addressed less to the mourner than to everyone around the mourner, translating an event that isolates one household into a sequence of obligations that the wider community could recognise and discharge. Its main work was coordination. Where such scripts have weakened, the result has not obviously been freer grief. Friends hesitate, unsure whether a call would comfort or intrude; colleagues say nothing for fear of saying the wrong thing; and the bereaved, told that they may grieve in their own way, often find that their own way is a lonely one, because nobody else knows what part to play in it.

This is not an argument for restoring every old rule, nor for pretending that the old forms were uniformly benign. Some customs plainly bore down hardest on those with least power, and a widow who was obliged to wear mourning for years was being policed as much as consoled. The lesson is narrower. A society that abandons shared forms for mourning does not thereby hand grief back to the individual; it removes the cues that let others accompany it. Any replacement worth having would keep that coordinating function while dropping the demand that inner feeling match an outward schedule.

options.B: settle in advance how relatives, neighbours and the bereaved household should conduct themselves after a death.

passage: Discussions of population ageing tend to begin with a single number. The old-age dependency ratio divides the number of people above a fixed age, usually sixty-five, by the number of people of working age, conventionally fifteen to sixty-four. As birth rates fall and lives lengthen the ratio rises, and a rising ratio is read as a growing burden: fewer shoulders, it is said, bearing the weight of more pensioners. The image is vivid and the arithmetic is simple, which is precisely why the measure deserves more suspicion than it usually receives.

The ratio rests on two equations that are rarely stated. The first is that everyone between fifteen and sixty-four supports others and everyone above sixty-five is supported by them. Neither half is true. Large numbers of people of working age are in education, unemployed, caring full-time for relatives or otherwise outside paid work, while many people beyond the threshold continue to earn, to pay taxes and, perhaps most importantly, to provide unpaid care. In many families it is grandparents whose looking after small children allows both parents to hold jobs; on the ratio's accounting, those grandparents appear only as a cost. The same error runs in the other direction for the many people in their fifties who have left paid work early through illness or redundancy, and who depend on others well before the line is reached.

The second equation is that a given age means the same thing in every generation. A sixty-five-year-old today in most countries can expect to live considerably longer, and in better health, than a sixty-five-year-old of the generation in which the threshold was fixed. To keep the line at sixty-five as life expectancy rises is to classify as old an ever larger share of people who are, by the standards that originally justified the line, not old at all. Some demographers have proposed measuring age prospectively, by the years a person can expect still to live rather than the years already lived; on such measures, populations age considerably more slowly than the headline ratio suggests.

None of this means that ageing is costless. The final years of a long life often bring a need for intensive medical and personal care, and as more people reach advanced old age that need grows in ways no redefinition can wish away. The objection is not to concern but to calibration. A measure that counts heads by birthday rather than activity by circumstance will tend to exaggerate the problem in its general form and to obscure it in the specific form, very late life, in which it is most acute.

passage: Among serious readers there is a settled suspicion of the happy ending. A novel that closes with a wedding, a reconciliation or a recovered fortune is assumed to have flinched at the last moment, to have given its audience what it wanted rather than what its story required. An ending in death, separation or failure, by contrast, is credited with courage. The assumption behind the contrast is rarely stated but easy to reconstruct: life does not resolve itself neatly, so a book that resolves neatly must be telling a comforting lie. The suspicion is old enough to have become a reflex, and few readers who share it could say where they acquired it.

There is something to this, since the history of popular fiction is crowded with endings that arrive from outside the story, the unexpected legacy, the villain who repents in a paragraph, the rival who conveniently dies, and readers are right to feel cheated by them. Such endings resemble a rescue by a passing stranger: welcome, perhaps, but unconnected with anything the characters have done. But the fault in such endings is not their happiness. It is that nothing in the preceding chapters made them necessary. A catastrophe imposed in the same way, a heroine killed by a runaway carriage because the author wanted the book to feel weighty, is no less arbitrary and, being arbitrary, no more truthful.

The prejudice persists, I think, because it confuses two things that endings do. Every ending closes; it marks the point after which the story will not be told. Some endings also console; they leave the reader reassured about the world the book has shown. Closure is a formal necessity, since a story must stop somewhere, while consolation is a choice. The suspicious reader notices that happy endings console, objects to the consolation, and then mistakes the objection for an argument against closure itself, as though the honest book would be the one that refused to finish. Yet an unhappy ending closes just as firmly; it simply closes on a different note, and that note can be just as comfortably familiar to readers who have learned to expect gloom from serious fiction.

The better test, then, is an internal one: an ending is honest when it is the place towards which the book's own pressures have been carrying it, so that a reader looking back can see how the earlier pages prepared it, whether that place is a marriage or a grave. By this test some happy endings are among the hardest-won things in fiction, and some tragic ones are merely fashionable. The question to ask of an ending is not whether it pleases but whether it follows.

passage: Cuteness is usually treated as the least serious of aesthetic qualities, if it is admitted to be an aesthetic quality at all. It belongs, we suppose, to stickers, toys and advertisements, and a taste for it is regarded as something to grow out of. Yet this dismissal sits oddly with the sheer power of the response. Few experiences in the visual world are as immediate or as hard to resist as the one produced by a large-eyed, round-faced, short-limbed creature stumbling towards us; we feel it before we have decided anything, and it is remarkably similar across cultures that agree on little else in matters of taste.

Students of animal behaviour noticed long ago that the features we find cute, a large head relative to the body, big low-set eyes, softness and clumsiness, are the features of the very young, and they proposed that the response is a mechanism for securing care. The explanation is plausible, but it accounts for less than it seems to. It tells us why infants elicit tenderness; it does not tell us why we find the same tenderness stirred by a cartoon kettle with eyes, or why the response is so readily extended to objects that need no care whatever. Once detached from the infant, the cute becomes a style, and a style can be applied to anything.

What makes the style interesting is its ambivalence. The cute object presents itself as small, soft and unable to resist, and our response to it is mixed in a way that tenderness towards a real child usually is not. Alongside the wish to protect, there is often a wish to possess and to handle, the half-joking urge to squeeze or pinch what one finds adorable, which people frequently admit to with some embarrassment. The cute flatters our power as much as it summons our care: it is an image of something that will never answer back.

This is why cuteness should be taken seriously rather than either indulged or sneered at. A quality that disarms judgement so quickly is a useful instrument for anyone who wishes to make something appear harmless, whether a product, an institution or a mascot standing in for an organisation whose activities are anything but soft. None of this means that delight in a kitten is a moral failing, and the pleasure is, in most of its forms, innocent enough. But an aesthetic that works by making us feel strong and kindly at once, and that does so before thought has begun, is not trivial; its very lightness is what gives it weight.

passage: For more than a century, the kilogram was a thing. Every measurement of mass in the world, from a pharmacist's dose to a shipping manifest, was ultimately traceable to a single cylinder of platinum and iridium kept under glass near Paris, against which official copies were periodically compared. When the definition was changed in 2019, so that the kilogram is now fixed by assigning an exact value to a fundamental constant of nature, the change was widely reported as the end of arbitrariness: the unit no longer depended on a lump of metal that someone had happened to cast.

That description gets the gain slightly wrong. The new definition is no less conventional in one obvious respect: the value assigned to the constant was chosen precisely so that the new kilogram would match the old one as closely as instruments could tell. Nobody wanted bags of flour to change weight overnight. Had the cylinder been cast a little heavier, the constant would have been given a different number. What the redefinition removed was not human choice but dependence on a particular object, and with it a peculiar kind of blindness.

The blindness worked like this. When the official copies were compared with the cylinder over the decades, they were found to have drifted apart from it by small but measurable amounts. Either the copies had gained mass, or the cylinder had lost it, or both; but because the cylinder was the kilogram by definition, there was no way, even in principle, to say that it had changed. A standard that defines itself cannot be found wanting. Whatever happened to it, it remained, officially, exactly one kilogram, and the masses of everything else silently moved with it. The world's weights were, in effect, being checked against a ruler that nothing could ever check.

A unit tied to a constant does not have this problem. Any sufficiently equipped laboratory can realise the kilogram from the definition, without travelling to a vault, and if two realisations disagree, the disagreement is a fact about the apparatus rather than about the unit. It must be admitted that the apparatus in question is elaborate, and only a handful of institutions can build it; in practice, most of the world still calibrates against physical masses, now traced to these laboratories rather than to Paris. Dependence has not disappeared. But it has become dependence on a procedure that can be checked and repeated, rather than on an object whose changes no one could ever detect.

passage: The sceptical argument about induction, usually traced to David Hume, has a disarming simplicity. Every inference from observed cases to unobserved ones assumes that the future will resemble the past, or more generally that nature is uniform. That assumption cannot be proved by logic, since its denial involves no contradiction, and it cannot be supported by experience without circularity, since the support would itself be an inference from observed cases. Philosophers have spent a long time looking for a way out, usually by searching for a single principle that would license inductive inference in general.

The search may be misconceived, because there is no such thing as inductive inference in general. Consider two investigators. One measures the melting point of a newly prepared sample of a pure compound and concludes, from a single careful trial, that every sample of that compound will melt at the same temperature. Another measures the height of one adult and draws no conclusion at all about the heights of adults. Both are reasoning well, and they differ not because one has found the universal principle and the other has not, but because each knows something about the kind of thing being studied: that pure compounds are uniform in their melting points, and that people are not uniform in their heights.

On this picture, what licenses an inductive step is not a principle of uniformity but particular facts about particular domains, which tell us how far a sample can be trusted to stand in for the whole. The obvious objection is that this merely relocates the problem. Our confidence that compounds are uniform in their melting points was itself acquired by induction, and so the sceptic can ask what licenses that.

The objection is fair, but it is less damaging than it looks, because it trades on an ambiguity between justifying each belief and justifying all of them together. The regress it describes is real, yet it never requires us to justify all our inductive habits at once. At any moment we lean on some background knowledge in order to test some other part of it, and any item can in turn be questioned while the rest is held fixed. This does not answer the sceptic on the sceptic's own terms, which demand a foundation lying outside experience altogether. It does show that the demand is not one that science, as actually practised, needs to meet in order to be rational, any more than a household needs to audit every account on the same afternoon in order to keep honest books.

passage: Few findings from the psychology of decision-making have travelled as far as the idea that too much choice is bad for us. The claim has a satisfying shape. It flatters the suspicion that modern abundance has not made people happier, and it offers a tidy remedy: fewer options, simpler shelves, shorter menus. Retailers have trimmed product lines in its name, and essayists have used it to diagnose a whole culture of anxious shoppers frozen before walls of nearly identical goods. Its appeal, in short, owes at least as much to its moral resonance as to the strength of the evidence on which it was originally built.

The evidence, however, is less tidy than the slogan. A handful of striking early experiments suggested that people offered many options were less likely to choose at all, and less satisfied when they did. Later attempts to reproduce such effects produced a far more mixed picture: sometimes the effect appeared, sometimes it vanished, and sometimes larger assortments made people more likely to buy. A finding that reverses under slightly different conditions is not a law of human nature. It is a clue that the conditions themselves are doing the work.

What might those conditions be? The more careful research points to a few. Large sets seem to burden people when they lack settled preferences in the domain, when the options differ along many dimensions that are hard to compare, when no option is marked as a sensible default, and when the decision feels consequential enough to invite later regret. A wine enthusiast choosing among forty bottles is browsing; a novice choosing among forty pension funds is drowning. The number of options is the same. What differs is whether the chooser has a way of sorting them, and therefore whether the abundance in front of him registers as an opportunity or as an accumulation of possible mistakes for which he alone will be answerable.

This reframing matters because it changes the remedy. If abundance itself were the problem, the answer would be to cut. If the problem is the absence of structure, the answer is often to organise: to group options by the features people care about, to supply defaults that can be overridden, to let people narrow the field in stages. Cutting still has its place, particularly when most of the options are poor or nearly identical. But a policy of reduction applied everywhere would deprive the enthusiast of what she values in order to rescue the novice from a difficulty that better design could have removed.

passage: A promise is an odd moral instrument. By uttering a few words, I create an obligation that did not exist a moment before, and I hand you a kind of authority over my future conduct. Because the obligation is self-made, it can seem absolute: having bound myself freely, I have no one to blame but myself if keeping my word turns out to be inconvenient. Much of the value of promising depends on this firmness. A promise that dissolved whenever the promiser found something better to do would offer the person relying on it nothing that a statement of intention does not already provide.

Yet no one seriously believes that every promise binds whatever happens. If I promise to meet you for lunch and, on the way, come upon an injured cyclist who needs to be taken to hospital, I should miss the lunch, and you would think less of me if I did not. The usual explanation is that the promise was outweighed: the duty to help the cyclist was simply stronger. But this explanation, though natural, misses something. It implies that I had two competing obligations and chose the heavier, leaving me in your debt for the one I failed to honour. In fact, most people would say that I owe you an explanation, perhaps an apology for your wasted time, but not compensation, and certainly not a confession of wrongdoing.

A better account starts from what was actually exchanged. When you accepted my promise, you did not acquire a right to my presence at lunch under every conceivable circumstance; you acquired a right against my changing my mind for reasons of my own convenience. Promises carry an implicit understanding of the conditions under which they were made, and both parties know, without saying so, that some emergencies fall outside it. On this view the cyclist does not outweigh the promise; he reveals that the promise never extended so far.

This account has a cost, and it should be admitted. If the scope of a promise is set by unspoken understandings, then a promiser who wants to escape can always claim that his circumstances fell outside what was understood. The firmness that made promising valuable seems to leak away. The answer is that the implicit conditions are not whatever the promiser privately had in mind; they are what a reasonable person in the promisee's position would have taken them to be. That standard will not settle every case, but it keeps the exceptions public, and a promise whose limits are public remains a promise worth having.

passage: Before the uniformed police forces that appeared in many large cities during the nineteenth century, the keeping of order was a patchwork. Night watchmen walked fixed rounds, parish constables served unpaid and often unwillingly, and private thief-takers recovered stolen goods for a fee, sometimes from the very thieves they claimed to pursue. What was new about the reformed police was not that they caught criminals more efficiently. It was the claim that a salaried, disciplined body of officers, visible on the street at all hours, could prevent offences from occurring at all. The patrol, rather than the arrest, was meant to be the core of the institution.

This founding idea has an awkward property: its successes cannot be seen. A burglary that does not happen leaves no record, and a street that stays quiet because an officer passed through it twenty minutes earlier looks exactly like a street that would have stayed quiet anyway. The arrest, by contrast, is countable. It produces a name, a charge and a figure that can be reported upward and compared from one year to the next. Over time, institutions tend to drift toward what they can count, and police forces have been no exception. Officers come to be judged by how many people they detain, and the quiet beat, which was supposed to be the whole point, comes to look like idleness.

It would be too simple to conclude that the preventive ideal was therefore an illusion. Critics sometimes point out that putting more officers on the street does not reliably reduce recorded crime, and they are right to be sceptical of large claims about deterrence. But the patrol was never only about deterrence. A visible and predictable presence tells residents that someone is responsible for the shared space of the street, and that sense of being looked after shapes whether people walk out at night, whether they report what they see, and whether they regard the police as theirs or as an occupying force. These effects are as hard to count as the burglary that did not happen, but they are not imaginary.

The deeper lesson concerns what happens when a public institution is measured by its most legible output rather than by its purpose. A force that rewards arrests will produce arrests, and it may do so in ways that erode the trust on which prevention depends. Recovering the original idea does not mean abandoning measurement; it means admitting that some of the most important things a police force does will show up, if at all, only as an absence.

passage: Generations of students have learned that science proceeds by a method, and that the method has steps. One observes, forms a hypothesis, designs an experiment, tests the hypothesis and draws a conclusion, after which the cycle begins again. The sequence is tidy, easy to examine and, as a description of what scientists actually do, very nearly useless. It is not that no scientist has ever followed it. It is that the sciences differ so widely in what they are able to do that any single recipe either excludes much of their work or becomes so general that it no longer guides anyone.

Consider the range. An astronomer studying a distant star cannot intervene in it; she can only watch, and her ingenuity lies in finding natural cases that differ in just the respect she wants to compare. A geologist reconstructing how a mountain range formed is not testing a hypothesis by experiment but assembling a history from traces, much as a detective does, and her standard of success is the coherence of a narrative that accounts for scattered evidence. A laboratory chemist may indeed run controlled experiments, but she spends much of her time on something the textbook sequence ignores entirely: making instruments and procedures work at all. To call all of this 'the scientific method' is to give one name to several distinct crafts.

The tidy sequence is not merely inaccurate; it does some damage. By making the controlled experiment the model of all good science, it encourages the view that sciences which cannot experiment are somehow lesser, as though reconstructing the history of the Earth were a provisional activity awaiting a proper laboratory. And by presenting science as a machine that turns hypotheses into conclusions, it leaves the public poorly prepared for the ordinary untidiness of research, in which results conflict, estimates are revised and experts disagree for long periods before they converge. People taught to expect the machine are apt to read each revision as a malfunction.

Is there, then, nothing that the sciences share? There is something, but it is not a procedure. What unites the astronomer, the geologist and the chemist is a set of habits about how claims are treated once they have been made: they are exposed to colleagues who are expected to attack them, they are stated in a form that evidence could tell against, and the people who make them are expected to give them up when such evidence arrives. These are norms of a community rather than steps for an individual, and that is precisely why they cannot be captured in a flowchart. A student who had absorbed them would understand science better than one who had memorised the steps, even if she could not say in what order they come.

passage: Arguments about the literary canon are usually conducted as arguments about a list. One side defends a set of books as the best that a tradition has produced; the other replies that the list was drawn up by a narrow group of readers and reflects their tastes and their blind spots. Both sides, for all their hostility, agree on what a canon is: a ranking, a roll of honour, a verdict on quality that can be revised by adding names or striking them out. It is worth asking whether that shared assumption is right.

A different account fits the actual history of canons better. On this account a work becomes canonical not because readers judge it excellent but because later writers cannot leave it alone. They answer it, parody it, borrow its situations, quarrel with its conclusions and rewrite it from the point of view of a character it neglected. The canonical work is then the one you must have read in order to understand a great many others; its status is less a medal than a position in a network of replies. This explains something the list model cannot. Canons contain works that almost everyone agrees are clumsy, uneven or dull in long stretches, and they exclude works of great finish that simply provoked no answer. A ranking by quality would not look like that; a record of a conversation would.

The account has a consequence for those who wish to change the canon. If canonical status is conferred by later writing rather than by verdict, then a syllabus committee cannot make a book canonical by placing it on a reading list, any more than a critic could remove one by declaring it overrated. What can be done is to put neglected works where future writers will meet them, in print, in translation and in the classroom, and then to wait and see whether they are taken up.

Yet the conversational canon is not thereby cleared of the exclusions its critics describe. Who gets to join a conversation depends on who was taught to read, who could find a publisher and whose replies were preserved. A tradition in which most writers came from one class or one sex will have conducted its conversation largely among them, and the canon it produced will reflect that. The conversational account does not answer the critics of the canon; it relocates their complaint, from the judgements of tastemakers to the conditions under which people could write at all, and that is where the remedy, if there is one, must be sought.

passage: Moral philosophers argue with cases. A theory is proposed, someone describes a situation in which the theory delivers a verdict that strikes nearly everyone as monstrous, and the theory is revised or abandoned. The practice treats our considered reactions to cases, usually called intuitions, as something like data: not infallible, but weighty enough that a principle which contradicts too many of them loses its claim on us. Critics have long found this method suspicious. Intuitions, they point out, are the residue of upbringing, culture and evolutionary pressures that had nothing to do with tracking moral truth. To test theories against them is to test a map against the traveller's prejudices about where the roads ought to go.

The objection has force, but it proves less than it seems to. Every method of inquiry begins with some judgements it does not, at that moment, question; the empirical sciences rely on perceptual reports whose reliability can be checked only by further perception. The question is not whether intuitions have causes unrelated to truth, for every belief has causes, but whether we have specific reason to think a particular intuition distorted. Sometimes we do. An intuition that tracks a vivid feature of a case, such as whether harm is done with one's own hands, while ignoring features that on reflection seem to matter more, such as how much harm is done, earns suspicion. But suspicion of that kind is itself grounded in other intuitions, about which features matter and which do not.

This is why the familiar picture of intuitions as raw data against which theories are tested is misleading in the other direction as well. The method that actually operates is one of mutual adjustment. Principles are revised in the light of judgements about cases, and judgements about cases are revised in the light of principles that have earned our confidence elsewhere. Neither level has final authority, and the goal is a state in which the two support each other. Critics sometimes say that this is circular, and in a sense it is; but the circle is wide, and it is not obvious that any inquiry into how we should live could proceed in a straight line.

What follows is a modest but not trivial conclusion. Intuitions are neither oracles nor noise. The debunker who dismisses them all owes us an account of the standpoint from which the dismissal is made, and it is hard to find one that does not rely on some judgement of the same kind. The defender who treats them as data owes us something too: a willingness to let a strong theory overturn a widely shared reaction, as moral thought has done before, when the reaction turns out to rest on a feature of cases that should never have mattered.

passage: The sterile worker castes of ants, bees and wasps troubled Darwin as much as almost any feature of the living world. A creature that never reproduces cannot pass on whatever traits make it a good worker, so it was hard to see how natural selection could have refined the elaborate behaviour of workers over many generations. Darwin's tentative answer was that selection might act on the family rather than on the individual, much as a breeder who wants a good strain of cattle keeps the relatives of an animal whose worth became clear only after it was slaughtered.

The idea was given a precise form only in the twentieth century. A gene that disposes its bearer to help relatives can spread even if the bearer leaves no offspring of its own, provided the help raises the reproduction of relatives who are likely to carry copies of the same gene. What matters is the product of two quantities, the benefit to the relative and the probability that the relative shares the gene, weighed against the cost to the helper. Sterility, on this account, is not an anomaly to be explained away but an extreme point on a continuum of helping, reached when a helper can do more for its genes by raising siblings than by raising young of its own.

For a time, a further detail seemed to make the case almost too neat. In ants, bees and wasps, males develop from unfertilised eggs, and a peculiarity of inheritance follows: sisters who share both parents are, on average, more closely related to one another than a mother is to her daughters. If workers are more closely related to their sisters than to their own potential offspring, raising sisters is the better genetic bargain, and sterile castes should arise readily in exactly these insects. The argument was elegant, and it was widely taught. It has not survived well. Termites, whose inheritance has no such peculiarity, have sterile castes too; the queens of many ants and bees mate with several males, which dilutes the relatedness among their daughters; and the great majority of species with this peculiar inheritance are not social at all.

The lesson is not that kinship is irrelevant. Workers in social insect colonies typically do raise relatives, and the general principle remains the best account of why they can afford to forgo reproduction. The lesson is rather that relatedness is only one term in the calculation. Ecological conditions that make independent breeding hopeless, such as a scarce nest site that must be defended or food that only a group can gather, raise the benefit of helping and can tip the balance even where relatedness is modest. The special feature of inheritance made a good story, but the more durable explanation lies in the interaction of kinship with circumstance.

options.C: Workers in social insect colonies typically raise relatives rather than unrelated young.
